list.listitem: Use Ottawa ankle rules to determine whether x-ray is necessary to rule out fracture. A
Use Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation (PRICE) mnemonic to guide conservative initial therapy. C
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and acetaminophen decrease pain and improve function. B
Functional therapy, including semirigid supports and early rehabilitation and balance training, is preferred to immobilization for the treatment of acute lateral sprains. B
Athletes with a history of recurrent sprains benefit most from prevention programs including proprioceptive training.C

background.definition: Acute ankle injuries include sprains, most commonly caused by lateral inversion, and fractures. Trauma to the ankle can result in fractures and high ankle sprains involve some tearing of the tibiofibular ligament.

list.listitem: Overall incidence of ankle injury is 1 per 100,000 persons per day, accounting for about 20% of all sports injuries.
The rate for collegiate athletes is 1.6 injuries for men and 2.2 for women per 1000 persons per day.
In 2004 Olympics, 54 total injuries per 1000 player matches; 29 of these injuries resulted in time lost from the sport.
Over 80% of ankle injuries are lateral ankle sprains.

Typical ankle sprain is an injury to the lateral ligaments occurring in the plantar flexed position, often from a fall or unsteady balance. The stabilizing ligaments (anterior talofibular, calcaneofibular, and posterior talofibular) are often injured in that order.
High ankle (tibiofibular syndesmosis) injuries often result from dorsiflexion and eversion of the ankle with tibial rotation.
Rarely, medial sided pain can result from injury to the deltoid ligament.
Fractures of the ankle and foot can occur with sufficient force.

There is a set of intrinsic functional and structural ankle deficits associated with significantly increased risk of ankle injury.The following are all associated with an increased risk of ankle injury: higher postural sway (SMD 0.693; 95% CI 0.151-1.235; p 0.012), being in the lower postural stability group (RR 2.06; 95% CI 1.364-3.111; p 0.001), lower inversion proprioception (0.573; 0.244-0.902; p <0.001).
Usually blunt trauma or a fall results in an inversion injury of the lateral ligaments, typically from a plantar flexed position.
Ankle support devices significantly decrease the risk of ankle sprains in those involved in high-risk sporting activities. B
A history of ankle sprains is likely to increase the risk of future sprains, particularly among active young athletes. C

Among high school athletes, inclusion of a balance training program reduces the incidence of ankle sprains (from 1.9 to 1.1 per 1000 practices); 26 athletes would have to be treated to prevent one sprain. Athletes with previous ankle sprains were twice as likely to suffer sprains.

Ankle support devices significantly decrease the risk of ankle sprains in high-risk sporting activities (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.40-0.69). Lace-up braces decrease the frequency but not severity of ankle injuries (NNT 15 to prevent one sprain in previously uninjured high-school basketball players).
Balance training and multi-intervention neuromuscular training decrease ankle sprains in adolescents and young adults.
A systematic review concluded that prophylactic programs reduced the risk of ankle sprain (OR 0.45; 95% CI 0.29-0.69).

Ankle bracing may not be effective to prevent lateral ankle sprains However studies show some benefit in competitive soccer players and military academy basketball players. A brace is more likely to be effective in people with prior sprain.

Ankle supports in the form of semi-rigid orthoses or air-cast braces are effective to prevent ankle sprains during high-risk sporting activities (e.g. soccer, basketball). Bracing has strong evidence to prevent recurrent ankle injury.

Overall taping, bracing and neuromuscular training were all effective for the prevention of ankle-sprain recurrences. The RRs of these prophylactic measures are of similar magnitude, ranging from 0.2 to 0.5 when compared with control groups. Although preventive effects have been reported in a general athletic population, evidence suggests this overall effect is due to a strong preventive effect in previously injured athletes and that any effect on fresh ankle sprains is either non-existent or very low.
A systematic review concluded that proprioceptive exercises reduce the incidence of ankle sprain in persons with (RR 0.64) and without (RR 0.57) previous ankle sprain.
Proprioceptive training is useful to prevent lateral ankle sprains, especially for those with prior sprains.
Moderate level evidence supports neuromuscular training to reduce recurrent ankle sprains.
Use Ottawa ankle rules to determine whether an ankle or foot x-ray is necessary to rule out fracture. A
Delayed physical examination may help to identify lateral ligament ruptures. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Proximal fibular or lateral talus fracture
Differential.Differential_Features: Pain, tenderness, localized swelling over/below the fibula, disruption of syndesmosis
Unusual persistent pain after several weeks, findings on magnetic resonance imaging or bone scan
Pain, swelling behind the fibula on lateral side
Inability to bear weight, evidence on radiographs

list.listitem: Ankle sprains can be graded from 1 to 3 ().

Use the Ottawa ankle and foot rules to help reduce unnecessary imaging. The Ottawa ankle rules are sensitive but not specific for fracture (negative likelihood ratio = 0.15). This rule is useful to rule out a fracture but there will be many false positives.

Delayed physical examination (3-5 days after injury) can detect lateral ligament rupture. Pain on palpation, bruising, and a positive anterior drawer test on delayed examination is 96% sensitive and 84% specific for lateral ligament rupture.
Urgent evaluation is recommended if there is a high level of pain, rapid swelling, coldness or numbness in the extremity, or a complicating condition such as diabetes.
Radiographs (anteroposterior, lateral, and mortise views) may be necessary to rule out fracture based on assessment using Ottawa ankle and foot rules.
The mortise view highlights the dome of the talus and helps to see if any syndesmotic disruption or tibial physis problems are present in a child.
If there is tenderness between the tibia and fibula, consider the possibility of a high ankle sprain or syndesmosis injury that may require imaging above the ankle.
Patients typically present with pain, swelling, and a history of recent trauma.
The mechanism of injury and onset of swelling time may give clues to the anatomic structure involved (ie, eversion vs inversion).
Ultrasound examination may provide useful information in patients with chronic pain after ankle sprain.
Ultrasound is sensitive and specific for detecting ankle fractures in an emergency department setting.

Ultrasound also has high diagnostic accuracy for acute lateral ankle ligament injury. anterior tibiofibular ligament injury sensitivity was 97% and specificity 93%. For calcaneofibular ligament they were 81% and 92% respectively.

Ottawa ankle rule: radiographs required only if there is pain at the posterior edge or tip of the lateral or medial malleolus (within 6 cm) and inability to bear weight both immediately and when presenting for care in the emergency department. This rule is also highly sensitive in children. It has a negative likelihood ratio of 0.12 for ruling out fracture when negative and is the most accurate decision tool.
Ottawa foot rule: radiographs are required only if there is pain at the base of the fifth metatarsal or navicular with difficulty with weight bearing immediately and in the emergency department.
See the Ottawa foot and ankle rules.
Standard regimen is PRICE.
Functional treatment, including semirigid or lace-up supports and balance training, superior to immobilization for return to function and reduced time off.
Standard regimen is PRICE. B
Intermittent icing may be more effective than continuous cryotherapy. B
NSAIDs are effective in reducing swelling and pain. B
Functional treatment, including semirigid or lace-up supports and balance training, superior to immobilization for return to function and reduced time off. B
No difference in long-term outcomes with conservative versus surgical therapy for lateral sprains. B
Army recruits randomized to piroxicam (Feldene) instead of placebo experienced less pain, had more endurance, and returned to duty more quickly.
Celecoxib (Celebrex or Celebra) is as effective as diclofenac in pain relief at day 4. Celecoxib and naproxen are also equally effective in ankle sprain pain relief.
Acetaminophen in adequate dose is as effective as ibuprofen for ankle sprain pain relief.

Diclofenac and paracetamol had the same effect on pain reduction of ankle sprains but more acute ankle edema was present in patients who were treated with diclofenac than in patients who were treated with paracetamol.

First line therapy is casting. Most ankle sprains, including Grade 3 injuries, can be managed without surgery.See chapter on "Fracture (leg)" for more information on treatment of tibial and fibular fracture.
A randomized trial (n=247) concluded that simple fibula fractures can be treated with splinting or casting for 3 weeks as opposed to casting for 6 weeks.

A trial randomized 669 adults with acute ankle fracture to a plaster cast or a removable brace. No statistically significant difference was found in the Olerud Molander ankle score between the cast and removable brace groups at 16 weeks (favours brace: 1.8, 95% confidence interval -2.0 to 5.6). No clinically significant differences were found in the Olerud Molander ankle scores at other time points, in the secondary unadjusted, imputed, or per protocol analyses.
Evidence is insufficient to decide on the effectiveness of surgery versus conservative treatment for nonfracture lateral ankle injuries.
One meta-analysis recommended surgical treatment for proven lateral ankle ligament rupture, especially for instability.
Functional outcomes for surgical vs. nonsurgical treatment of closed, unstable ankle fractures are equivalent.

This is also true in older adults with closed unstable ankle fracture. A randomized trial of 620 adults 60 years and older with this injury found that conservative management was at least as effective as surgical management, with similar pain, function, patient satisfaction, quality of life, mobility and fewer infections.
Early weight-bearing, within 3 weeks, leads to better outcomes after surgery for ankle fracture. Removable ankle support may also improve outcomes after surgery.
Patients casted after surgery may have fewer cutaneous complications though not casting after surgery is also an option.

Patients hospitalized following open treatment of ankle fracture had higher complication rates than those treated as outpatients (especially surgical site infection and pulmonary embolism), although this may in part be due to confounding with higher risk patients hospitalized post-operatively.

For distal fibula ankle fractures, a systematic review of 4 studies with 262 patients compared open reduction interal fixation with locked intramedullary nailing (IMN). IMN was favored in terms of outcomes a complications.
Ultrasound therapy is not effective for ankle sprains.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is not helpful for ankle sprains and may increase muscle soreness within 2 to 3 days.
There is no evidence to support acupuncture for acute ankle injury.
More patients returned to sports and work sooner and were more satisfied if they received functional treatment.

A Cochrane review identified 53 studies of 4489 adults with ankle fracture. They concluded (12 studies) that early weight bearing probably leads to better ankle function although the benefit is modest. After surgery, removable ankle supports are preferred over non-removable supports based on 25 studies. After non-surgical management, there is probably no difference between removable and non-removable. The certainty for the efficacy of PT interventions such as active controlled motion, a spring‐loaded ankle trainer, an antigravity treadmill, and variations of enhanced physiotherapy was low and meta-analysis was not possible.
In lateral ankle sprain, additional supervised ankle exercises can hasten return to work and sport.
Early mobilization is effective.
Ankle circles, alphabet letters, and toe and heel raises are easily performed and very effective.
Injuries can be reduced by incorporating exercises specifically aimed at improving proprioception, strength, and balance.
A semirigid support resulted in faster returns to sports and work and less instability than an elastic bandage.
Proprioceptive exercises reduce the incidence of ankle sprains in patients with previous injury.
Supervised exercises are no better than advice alone for rehabilitation after ankle fracture.
Home exercise programs are a reasonable alternative to supervised exercise program and cost less.

Although braces are recommended for injury prevention purposes, the impact of braces on physical performance is unknown. No restrictions were observed with running, climbing, jumping, or negotiating obstacles. Lace-up ankle braces can be used in conjunction with combat boots to protect the ankle during high-risk activities without having an impact upon tactical movements.
A systematic review found that early physical therapy does not improve recovery from acute mild to moderate ankle sprain.

For the subset of patients with chronic complaints after ankle sprain, a systematic review concluded that training programs yield better functional and pain outcomes than wait and see or no treatment.
Icing may be effective immediately after injury, but high-quality randomized controlled trials are lacking.

Intermittent ice therapy resulted in improvement of pain immediately after injury compared with a continuous protocol, with pain score 1 (95% CI 0.8-1.2) compared with 1.7 (1.5-1.9). There was no difference in pain after 1 week, and functional status was similar.
Rehabilitation is an important part of treatment.
Goals are to speed return to usual activity and prevent recurrence.
See for a 3-phase approach to rehabiliation.
With acute ankle or foot fracture, consider evidence of nerve injury or tears of the peroneal tendons.
Refer if there is failure to improve in 6 to 8 weeks without an obvious reason.
More patients will typically recover on their own from grade 1 sprains. Grade 2 sprains often require more intense interventions. C
Use of semirigid supports and training rehabilitation program reduce risk of future injury and hasten recovery. B
Chronic pain, ankle instability, and arthritis can result from severe ankle sprains that are left untreated or not diagnosed properly.
Patients will typically recover on their own from grade 1 sprains.
Grade 2 sprains often require more intense interventions. Some range of movement (ROM) and proprioceptive deficits may remain for several months afterward.
It is unclear whether severe sprains or ruptures benefit more from surgery or conservative outcomes.
Patients failing to improve with treatment within 6 weeks should be considered for referral or reevaluation.

Patients with a more severe index sprain are more likely to have chronic ankle instability. A systematic review of four studies found that this was the only predictor, and that postural control or perceived instability were not predictive.
Athletes suffering a significant inversion injury should continue in an ankle support for up to 6 months if they continue to participate.
Rehabilitation and functional training should begin as soon as possible to regain ROM and prevent reinjury.
Pay special attention to the alignment of the lower extremities and the tibial and fibular physes when examining children.
Ottawa ankle rules are accurate in children.
Children suffering from ankle injuries have nearly half the dorsiflexion range as a control group, even in the uninjured ankle.
Non-restraint (compared to a functional bandage) is an acceptable option in pediatric ankle sprain.

Pain higher up in the fibula

Exercises to increase peroneal or dorsiflexion strength, proprioception, stretching of Achilles tendon with goal of gaining up to 80% of normal strength
